data.name: King of the World
data.detailed_description:
JOIN OUR DISCORD


Acerca do jogo



Welcome to a world of skillfull commanders, cunning tacticians and backstabbing schemers.

Balanced Gameplay

Become the winner by outsmarting your opponents or simply conquer them by force. It doesn't matter if you're a tactical genius or a novice, all players will start each game with the same conditions.

Different Armies

Chose between 3 different armies from 3 different eras each offering an unique playstyle to find the one that suits you the best, perform well in-game and several skins can be obtained to get even more unique.

Technology Tree

Features a unique technology tree for each army, gain technology points every 5 turns that you can use to enhance your strategies.

12 Player Free for all

Engage in 12 player battles where everyone is against each other, or simply create a custom game to play with less or bring your friends to play in any kind of team composition you'd like.

Control regions to increase your income

Take control of all points in a region to increase your income with the amount of points in the region, controlling regions will grant you additional reinforcements.

Balanced Gameplay

Become the winner by outsmarting your opponents or simply conquer them by force. It doesn't matter if you're a tactical genius or a novice, all players will start each game with the same conditions.

Leveling System

Gain experience points after each match, gain in game currency after each level, special skins or loading borders each milestone up to level 100.

Welcoming Community

Join our new player friendly community, get tips on how to play or find a friend. Discord link in the Forum.

Previously included in the Definitive Edition but now free for everyone!

  • Singleplayer Campaign - Experience our singleplayer campaign with an epic story.
  • Map Editor - Create your own maps, and share them for everyone to play!
  • Ability to create custom games.

data.short_description: King of the World is the gameplay from RISK in a Real-time strategy setting. Fight up to 12 players at once while scheming, backstabbing, making shallow alliances or simply conquer to become the last man standing.

reviews.review:
King of the World approaches territorial strategy with a clever mixture of board-game-inspired conquest and real-time competition. Rather than focusing exclusively on rapid unit production and mechanical micromanagement, it places considerable importance on controlling territory, anticipating rival intentions, and deciding when cooperation is more valuable than aggression. Developed and published by Contec Games, the game revolves around becoming the dominant power on the battlefield, but reaching that position can involve diplomacy, temporary alliances, deception, and outright military force. This combination gives matches a social and political character that helps distinguish the experience from conventional real-time strategy games.

The basic structure is deliberately accessible. Players begin under equal conditions, meaning that success is primarily determined by decisions made during the match rather than predetermined advantages. Expansion is important because controlling complete regions improves income and provides additional reinforcements, creating a natural incentive to capture strategically connected areas instead of attacking without direction. The system encourages careful planning because expanding too aggressively can produce an empire that is powerful on paper but difficult to defend. Meanwhile, concentrating too heavily on defense may allow another commander to accumulate enough territory and resources to become a serious threat.

Large multiplayer battles are where the concept becomes particularly interesting. Matches can accommodate as many as twelve players, while custom games allow smaller groups and different team arrangements. With numerous commanders competing simultaneously, relationships can change quickly. Two players might cooperate against a dominant opponent before immediately turning against each other once that common threat disappears. Alliances therefore feel more like temporary strategic arrangements than permanent commitments. The possibility of betrayal complements the territorial mechanics nicely, since players must consider not only where enemy armies are positioned but also which rivals are likely to attack next.

There are three armies drawn from different eras, and each offers its own playstyle and technology tree. Technology points are periodically earned and can be invested to strengthen particular strategies, adding a progression layer within individual matches. Although three armies may sound modest compared with strategy games containing enormous faction rosters, the focused selection makes the differences easier to understand. Choosing technologies according to the current political and military situation can also create meaningful decisions. A strategy that works when surrounded by weaker opponents may become ineffective when facing an organized alliance or a rapidly expanding rival.

Progression extends beyond individual battles. Experience gained after matches contributes toward player levels, with in-game currency, skins, and loading borders providing rewards as progress continues. These additions do not replace the central strategy mechanics, but they give regular players something persistent to pursue. Cosmetic customization also helps differentiate armies visually without fundamentally undermining the game's emphasis on relatively balanced starting conditions.

The available modes make the package broader than its multiplayer-focused premise initially suggests. A single-player campaign provides a story-driven alternative for anyone wanting structured scenarios, while online PvP and cooperative options remain available for more unpredictable competition. The map editor is another worthwhile inclusion because players can construct battlefields and share their creations, potentially extending variety beyond the standard maps. Custom game creation is similarly valuable for groups that prefer specific player counts or team configurations. These features were previously associated with additional content but are now presented as available to everyone, substantially strengthening the core package.

Presentation is relatively straightforward, but that suits a game where battlefield readability matters more than visual spectacle. Territorial borders, armies, and strategic locations need to remain understandable while several factions are competing simultaneously. The maps provide an appropriate stage for the shifting balance of power, while the background music and sound effects support the action without overwhelming it. Much of the excitement comes from watching the strategic situation evolve rather than from elaborate cinematic effects. Seeing a rival unexpectedly capture an important region or discovering that an apparent ally has begun concentrating forces near your territory can create tension naturally through gameplay.

The streamlined nature of the design can also be a limitation depending on expectations. Players seeking the extensive base management, enormous unit rosters, intricate resource chains, or intense micromanagement associated with more complicated RTS titles may find this comparatively lightweight. Its greater strength lies in combining territorial conquest with diplomacy and multiplayer unpredictability. Consequently, the quality of a match can depend significantly on the participants. A competitive group willing to negotiate, betray, cooperate, and react strategically can generate memorable situations, whereas less active opponents may expose the relative simplicity underneath the political layer.

Steam Deck support is a welcome advantage. The game is rated Playable rather than fully Verified, and its default controller configuration provides access to the complete functionality while the default graphics configuration performs appropriately on the handheld. There are still compromises: some interface elements can display mouse, keyboard, or non-Steam-Deck controller icons, certain text may appear small on the Deck's screen, and text entry can require manually opening the virtual keyboard. Single-player also requires an active internet connection. Despite these inconveniences, the game runs successfully through SteamOS and remains a practical handheld option, particularly for players willing to tolerate occasional interface friction.

Overall, King of the World succeeds most when treated as an accessible territorial strategy game driven by human unpredictability rather than as a deeply technical traditional RTS. Region control, reinforcements, technology development, multiple armies, progression, custom battles, a campaign, and map creation provide enough interconnected systems to give the straightforward conquest premise variety. Its greatest attraction is the uncertainty created by competing commanders: today's useful ally can easily become tomorrow's greatest threat. The strategic systems could offer greater depth, but their simplicity also makes the game easier to approach and keeps attention focused on expansion, diplomacy, timing, and betrayal. For players who enjoy Risk-like world domination concepts but want them presented through a faster real-time format, it offers an entertaining and distinctive interpretation of territorial warfare.

Rating: 7/10
